newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu battles rebellious allies.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu battles rebellious allies.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu struggled to placate rebellious political allies hoping to avert a no-confidence vote in parliament on Tuesday.

Little more than a year into office, the 47-year-old prime minister found himself under pressure from coalition parties demanding action on promises and control of ministries he is due to dish out in a cabinet reshuffle.
"Regrettably, we are talking about a huge number of personal and selfish interests," said Michael Eitan, the member of parliament from Netanyahu's rightist Likud party who acts as coalition chief.
By all accounts Netanyahu would defeat the no-confidence votes scheduled for Tuesday in the 120-seat Knesset and brought by opposition parties critical of his administration.
Netanyahu voiced confidence on Monday his opponents would fall short of the 61 votes required to force new elections for both prime minister and parliament.
"We have a government which will continue. The coalition is stable. There are problems -- they'll be solved," he said.
It remained to be seen however how many of the coalition members who make up Netanyahu's 66-54 majority would abandon him as a number of disaffected comrades threatened to abstain.

It was even unclear who would defend the government in parliament before the votes since the woman assigned to the job, Communications Minister Limor Livnat, angrily resigned on Saturday as coordinator between the government and parliament.
Netanyahu's spokesman said the Israeli leader still intended to put his new ministerial appointments to votes in cabinet and parliament also on Tuesday.
Ex-general Ariel Sharon was frontrunner for the senior job of finance minister vacated by Netanyahu's Likud party rival Dan Meridor last week in a power struggle over the economy.

Netanyahu's judgment has come into question on issues ranging from Jewish settlement expansion which has plunged Middle East peacemaking into crisis to a political appointment which nearly got him indicted earlier this year.
Israeli political analysts cite Netanyahu's inexperience and massive ambition as possible explanations.
"The only solution is early elections," insisted David Magen, a member of parliament from the Likud-Gesher-Tsomet alliance who quit as Netanyahu's deputy finance minister.

The biggest threat to Netanyahu's government appeared to come from a party of Russian immigrants led by former Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky demanding say over the next ambassador to Moscow and aid for constituents.
"As long as we don't get real answers, we won't be able to vote for the prime minister," said Roman Bronfman, leader of Sharansky's seven-member Yisrael ba-Aliya faction in parliament.
But Shimon Shiffer, diplomatic correspondent of Israel's biggest newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said there was no way 61 members of parliament would come out against Netanyahu.
"Basically the members of his coalition feel very good that they are now running the country and have all these budgets. No one really seriously wants to go to a new election," he said.

"What they want is more budgets and more power and it's just a legitimate way to get it until tomorrow and that is what they are doing. It seems very ugly, but this is the way of politics in every democracy -- to try what you can when you can."
Sharon's expected appointment has stirred controversy. Critics fear he will exploit the job to expand Jewish settlement viewed by Washington as an obstacle to peace.
It would be Sharon's most senior cabinet post since a 1982 Beirut massacre of Palestinians forced him out as defence minister in 1983.
